chapter_theme: In the second run of the debate with Mokkalan, Neelakesi defends the Jain existents of motion and rest, space and time, the soul of the body's size, its bondage, its passage between births and the persistence of things through change, against Buddhist objections she restates and answers; the run ends, in a shorter metre, with her attack on the Buddhist excuses for eating meat killed by others.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist teacher Neelakesi debates in the மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம்

292.reading: Neelakesi sets out the charge that the Jain counts do not agree with one another (if the existents are five, the six substances are not they, and neither tallies with the nine categories recited), and closes by asking whether the opponent, who hides and shows his own things at will, has an account that holds together any better.
292.nuance: The five அத்தி (astikayas), the six substances and the nine categories are three standard Jain lists that overlap rather than compete; the charge treats them as rival totals. The answer is the run of verses that follows (293 to 296), which explains dharma and adharma, two of the five, and turns on the Buddhist's own list. Who frames the charge is not fully clear from the verse alone, though it closes with என்றாள்.

claims.claim: the Jain counts of five extended existents, six substances and nine categories contradict one another

293.reading: Neelakesi says the opponent twisted the Jain teaching into 'we move by dharma': the Jains say only that where dharma is lacking there is no motion, for dharma lets moving things go as the sea lets a ship go, without pushing it as the wind does, and good teaching turns in him to poison like milk a snake has drunk.
293.nuance: The refuted claim is the opponent's version of the Jain doctrine, which Neelakesi calls a quibble (சலம்); the Jain view as she gives it separates a condition of motion (the sea) from its cause (the wind).

claims.claim: dharma is the force that drives moving things
dharma is the medium without which nothing moves, not the mover itself

294.reading: Neelakesi says the opponent will not accept that adharma stands to rest as dharma stands to motion, and mocks him for wearing out his mouth repeating 'going and making go, staying and making stay' until he rubs his teeth too.
294.nuance: அல்லதற்கம் stands for adharma (the existent of rest). The pairs செல்லவும் செலுத்தவும், நில்லவும் நிறுத்தவும் are the opponent's confusion of a thing's own going or staying with being made to go or stay.

claims.claim: adharma is the medium of rest as dharma is of motion, not the cause that makes things stay

295.reading: Neelakesi answers the opponent's question why sea, land and space are not enough, and what is lost if dharma and adharma do not exist: if they did not, the world would have no edge, and the room of souls and matter would spill past every bound.
295.nuance: புற்கலம் is pudgala, matter. The Jain argument is cosmological: space is unbounded, so something other than space must mark where the inhabited world ends.

claims.claim: dharma and adharma are superfluous, since sea, land and space suffice for things to move and rest
dharma and adharma fix the limit of the world within which souls and matter can move

296.reading: Neelakesi says the opponent needs no long speech to be shown short: he admits only the five great aggregates, has no space of measureless extent, needs no conditions of rest and motion, and so, setting out to state the world's limit, only strains his own understanding.
296.nuance: பஞ்சமா கந்தம் is the Buddhist list of five aggregates. That the Buddhist denies space as an entity is the Jain's report; the answer is that without space and the existents of motion and rest he cannot say where the world ends.

claims.claim: only the five aggregates are real, and space is no entity

297.reading: Neelakesi mocks the opponent for denying time while speaking without shame of moments, aeons and ages, and of a man as child, scholar and old ascetic in turn, and asks whether he is deluded or has eaten something that dazes him.
297.nuance: காலம் here is time as one of the Jain substances, not the Kural's right season. கணிகம், the moment, is the Buddhist's own word for momentariness, so the barb is that his central doctrine presupposes the time he denies.

claims.claim: time is not a real thing
one who denies time cannot speak of moments, aeons or the stages of a life

298.reading: Neelakesi says that where the Jains, watching the heavenly bodies rise, take them as marking time, the opponent watches the same bodies, sees them only as themselves and says there is no time at all, though he counts and praises years by them; she sees no way to correct such excess by sound doctrine.
298.nuance: கோள் may mean the planets or the tenets of the two sides; the reading as heavenly bodies fits the counting of years (ஆண்டு எண்ணி).

claims.claim: there is no time beyond the risings of the heavenly bodies

299.reading: To the opponent's charge that the Jains fabricate what they neither inferred nor saw, Neelakesi answers that on that rule there could be no medical treatise to cure disease, and tells him to stop speaking in confusion and correct his own want of understanding.
299.nuance: கருத்து is inference and கண்கூடு perception, the two means of knowledge the Buddhist logicians allow; Neelakesi's counter-instance is a body of knowledge that rests on texts.

claims.claim: only what is perceived directly or inferred is known; anything else is fabrication
an authoritative text is a means of knowledge, as the medical treatise that cures disease shows

300.reading: Neelakesi takes up the opponent's rule that the soul knows only matter within the senses' range and that what such knowing does not reach cannot exist, and asks him to say, without scripture, whether Indra's queen in his far city is short or tall.
300.nuance: The taunt works because the Buddhist too speaks of Indra and his heaven, which no sense has reached; Neelakesi turns his own cosmology into testimony he relies on.

claims.claim: the soul knows only matter that the senses reach, and what they do not reach does not exist
what lies beyond the senses is known only through scripture

301.reading: Neelakesi takes up the objection that a soul of the body's size cannot be held inside the body, any more than one pot fits inside another of its measure, and answers that the opponent himself holds that consciousness, of the body's extent, is held within the body, so to deny the same of the self is a fool's way.
301.nuance: The Jain soul takes the size of the body it occupies. ஆதன் (fool) and the pot image (அளவைக் குடம்) are both slightly obscure; the parity argument with consciousness is clear.

claims.claim: a soul as large as the body cannot be contained within the body
the soul extends through the whole body and is contained within it

302.reading: Neelakesi says that if the opponent explains consciousness as contained in the body because it is formless, there is no great dispute, since the Jains say the same of the soul, but asks how on his account formless consciousness can have contact, union, mixture or binding with a body that has form.
302.nuance: திருவாளன் is ironic. The verse turns the opponent's problem (how is a formless soul bound?) back on his own account of consciousness and body.

claims.claim: being formless, the soul is held in the body as formless consciousness is

303.reading: When Neelakesi says that if there is bondage it is the soul that suffers, the opponent answers that when the body-mass suffers there is no 'I' to lament; she asks whether his doctrine is then that a man struck by an arrow cries 'I am wounded to death' for a pain that belongs to strangers.
303.nuance: பிண்டம் is the lump of the body, the Buddhist's bundle without a self. Line 3 (ஏதிலர்க்காய்ச் சோமாகி) does not construe cleanly.

claims.claim: where there is bondage it is the soul that suffers
suffering belongs to the bodily aggregate and to no self

304.reading: Neelakesi says the opponent stumbles on the high road by not seeing that 'by my acts I came to grief' is an error on his own terms, and that those who hold feeling, cognition, perception and action to belong to one being have nothing here to answer for.
304.nuance: உழப்பு, அறிவு, குறி, செய்கை are four of the five Buddhist aggregates (feeling, consciousness, perception, formations), the non-bodily ones. Neelakesi does not deny the list; she gives all four one owner, which is what the Buddhist denies.

claims.claim: feeling, cognition, perception and volition belong to a single subject

305.reading: Neelakesi repeats the dilemma the opponent levels at the Jains (a formless soul cannot be bound, and a soul with form would be diminished, so either way fails) and says he has not taken in what was said to him and grasps no comparison however it is put.
305.nuance: The answer she says he ignores is the parity argument of 302: his own formless consciousness is held in the body.

claims.claim: a formless soul cannot be bound and a soul with form would be diminished, so the soul is untenable either way

306.reading: Neelakesi calls it great folly, not the word of those who know, to say that cognition arises and itself suffers and that as it arises something else is bewildered, says the opponent seizes only on faults, and taunts him to trap the wind in a machine.
306.nuance: The target seems to be a momentary cognition taken as subject of suffering; what பிறிதொன்று names is unclear, and so is the point of the wind-trap taunt.

claims.claim: a cognition arises and is itself what suffers, while another thing is confused

307.reading: To the objection that no one carries the soul, it does not walk, and deeds cannot convey it, so the doer of good can hardly reach the world of the gods, Neelakesi answers that he speaks from outside the doctrine: does not the whirligig turn when the wind strikes it?

claims.claim: since nothing carries the soul, the doer of good cannot travel to the world of the gods
deeds move the soul to its next birth as the wind turns a whirligig

308.reading: Neelakesi takes up the dilemma about the one reborn (if he is the same man his great sorrow has no end, and if he is not, the good he did is wasted) and says the question 'who then becomes?' only states the Jain position, mocking the opponent for hiding himself in broad daylight to escape the laughter.
308.nuance: The dilemma suits a Buddhist attack on a persisting soul, and the reply that it states the Jain view suggests the Jain answer of a self both same and changed (see 312); but whose dilemma it is and how எமது இட்டமே is meant are not certain.

claims.claim: if the one reborn is the same man his sorrow never ends, and if not, the good he did is wasted

309.reading: To the opponent's demand that she say how a body is gained if the soul leaves the dead body with only its karma-body and no body has been laid in the mother's, Neelakesi answers that he fails to see the fiery body, like a shadow, entering another body.
309.nuance: வினையுடம்பு and தேயுடம்பு are the Jain karmic and fiery (taijasa) bodies that go with the soul between births. Line 4 begins with டேயுடம்பு where தேயுடம்பு is expected.

claims.claim: a soul leaving the dead body with only its karma-body cannot gain a new body unless one is set in the mother's
a subtle fiery body enters the new body as a shadow does

310.reading: Neelakesi explains that things give room to one another as heated iron takes in water, and that the soul, embracing the father's seed and the mother's blood, settles within the body like ghee in plaster and grows along with it.

claims.claim: the soul takes up the parents' seed and blood, settles within the body and grows with it

311.reading: Neelakesi says the Jains need neither of the opponent's alternatives, that a deed bears fruit only while it stands or ripens only when it has wholly perished, because a deed, when explained, has persistence, arising and destruction at once.
311.nuance: நிலை, தோற்றம், நாசம் is the Jain triad of persistence, origination and destruction. ஐவினை in line 4 is obscure (fine, subtle, or a division error).

claims.claim: a deed must yield its fruit either while it persists or after it has wholly perished
a deed, like every existent, has persistence, arising and destruction together

312.reading: Neelakesi gives the example of a gold pot broken and made into a jewelled crown, where the gold persists while one form is lost and another made, and says that men and gods are souls in the same way, so the opponent should not think it idle talk that the Jains repeat daily.

claims.claim: as gold persists while the pot perishes and the crown arises, the soul persists through births as man or god

313.reading: In a shorter metre, Neelakesi tells the Buddhists that if killing is a sin, it reaches the eater too, and rejects their claim that sin goes and joins only where there is intention.
313.nuance: The verse addresses the Buddhists in the plural (புத்தரே நீவிர்). குறட்கண்ணும் in line 1 is obscure, and the eater is supplied from the argument of 314 rather than named here.

claims.claim: the sin of killing does not attach where there is no intention to kill
if killing is a sin, it reaches also the one who eats what was killed

314.reading: Neelakesi takes up the opponent's rule about eating, after renunciation, what others have cooked, and asks whether he does not count himself an ascetic while eating what a woman he has renounced has cooked.
314.nuance: சூனை (slaughter, or the place of killing and cooking) and the construction of lines 1 and 2 are uncertain; the argument appears to be that the Buddhist ascetic eats meat cooked by householders and denies any share in the killing.

claims.claim: a renouncer who eats what others have prepared does not share the fault of its preparing

315.reading: Neelakesi says that if the opponent claims the sin of killing is undone by raising the hand and saying 'let it perish', he says it as a fool, and tells him to go back and forth into his meditation.
315.nuance: The last line is sarcasm about Buddhist meditation as a cure for a killing that has already happened. Whether the gesture is a real Buddhist rite or the debater's caricature the verse does not show.

claims.claim: the sin of killing is removed by raising the hand and declaring it gone

316.reading: Neelakesi takes up the question what fault there is in holding that pleasure and pain are the effects of the two kinds of deeds, and answers that on that view the suffering of the penance one later undertakes falls under the same rule.
316.nuance: The verse can be read either as the Buddhist objection that penance's pain is only old karma ripening, which would make penance pointless, or as Neelakesi turning that objection; line 4 (துதாங்கனத் தொன்றுமே) is corrupt and the answer is not given here.

claims.claim: pleasure and pain are the effects of good and bad deeds
on that view the pain of penance undertaken later is itself only the fruit of deeds

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain speaker says dharma pervades everything and makes things move (பொருள்களை நடத்தும்); Neelakesi calls the reading 'we move by dharma' a quibble and says dharma lets things move as the sea lets a ship go, without pushing.
links.teaches: A Jain debater rejects as a misreading the very wording a Buddhist epic puts in a Jain's mouth: dharma is a condition of motion, not a mover, a distinction the Buddhist report blurs.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain says time makes the short occurrence called கணிகம் and the long one of கற்பம்; Neelakesi throws the same two words at the Buddhist who denies time while using them.
links.teaches: The pair கணிகம் and கற்பம் was the Jain definition of time, so when Neelakesi mocks the Buddhist for speaking of moments she is pointing out that the word for his momentariness belongs to a doctrine of time he rejects.

links.note: Both give the Jain doctrine that a thing persists in kind while its form arises and perishes: the Manimekalai's Jain with gram cooked into a dish and the sprouting neem, Neelakesi with a gold pot remade as a crown, applied to the soul passing from man to god.
links.teaches: On arising, persistence and destruction the Buddhist epic's report of the Jains matches a Jain debater's own illustration, so here the polemical account is one the school would accept, and the Neelakesi shows it was aimed at the soul's rebirth.

links.note: Neelakesi says the Buddhist has no space of measureless extent; the Manimekalai's teacher of logic names both 'one who says space is unreal' and 'one who says it is real' as parties to an argument, without taking a side there.
links.teaches: The Buddhist manual treats the reality of space as a disputed thesis between parties, while the Jain debater fixes the denial on the Buddhist and draws its cost, that the world then has no edge.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the first Jina (in Buddhist usage, the Buddha) taught only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Neelakesi answers that on that rule there could be no medical treatise that cures disease.
links.teaches: The Buddhist rule of two means of knowledge, stated as doctrine in one epic, meets in the other a counter-case from medicine, showing that the dispute over scripture as a means of knowledge was argued in Tamil from practical knowledge, not only from revelation.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) as what is spoken of as a person; Neelakesi names feeling, cognition, perception and action (உழப்பு, அறிவு, குறி, செய்கை) and says they belong to one being.
links.teaches: The Jain debater accepts the Buddhist list of the four mental aggregates term for term and disputes only whether they have one owner, so the quarrel over the self is about ownership of the aggregates, not about what they are.

links.note: In the opening sermon the sage tells the worshippers that a child's body comes from blood and its life from former deeds; here Neelakesi explains how the soul takes up the father's seed and the mother's blood and grows within the body.
links.teaches: The sage's bare division between a body from the parents and a life from former deeds is filled in by the debate with the mechanism of conception that lets the Jain deny any god a part in it.

links.note: Neelakesi says that if only perception and inference counted there could be no medical treatise; the Kural's chapter on medicine states the three humours on the authority of the learned in the books (நூலோர்).
links.teaches: The Kural's deference to the medical books for the three humours is just the kind of text-borne knowledge the Jain debater cites: neither the patient's sight nor his inference gives it.

gains.a: the debater's appeal to medicine gets a Tamil instance in which a moral book takes medical doctrine on its authors' word
gains.b: the couplet's passing reference to நூலோர் is seen to carry a view of knowledge that a rival school in Tamil denied

links.note: Neelakesi rejects the Buddhist rule that the sin of killing attaches only where there is intention; the Kural argues that if none killed to eat, none would sell flesh for a price.
links.teaches: The Kural's buyer-and-seller argument is the reply the intention defence needs: the eater need intend no killing for his eating to cause one, so a rule that weighs only intention misses the chain from buyer to slaughter.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare charge that the sin reaches the eater gets a causal argument behind it
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed opponent is identified as a live doctrine, that sin requires the intent to kill

links.note: The objection in Neelakesi 316 is that if pleasure and pain are the fruit of deeds, the pain of penance is too; the Kural defines penance as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life.
links.teaches: The Kural's definition of தவம் as bearing the pain that comes takes away the force of the objection: if penance is endurance of what arrives, it does not matter that the pain is old karma's fruit.

gains.a: the epic's objection meets a Tamil definition of penance that already answers it
gains.b: the couplet's உற்றநோய் is shown to bear on a live dispute about whether penance's pain is only karma ripening

links.note: Neelakesi says deeds move the soul to its next birth as the wind turns a whirligig; Tirumular says the subtle breath in the soul carries it as wind carries a flower's scent.
links.teaches: Both answer what carries a soul between bodies with an image of wind, but for the Jain the wind is the deed itself, needing no other mover, while for Tirumular it is the vital breath at the appointed moment, so the same image names karma in one and breath in the other.

gains.a: the whirligig image is set against a Tamil alternative it leaves out, breath as the carrier
gains.b: Tirumular's image is seen as one answer to a question a rival school answered with deeds alone

links.note: Neelakesi's fiery body enters another body like a shadow; Tirumular's light born in the womb spreads through the earthly body like a bubble in water, a shadow, and the eight take hold.
links.teaches: Writers of opposed schools both picture the subtle body that passes into a new one as a shadow, which shows they agreed rebirth needs a subtle carrier and differed only on what it is made of, the Jain fiery and karmic bodies or Tirumular's eight.

gains.a: the Jain doctrine of the subtle bodies is seen to have a Saiva counterpart, so the debate does not turn on whether a subtle body exists
gains.b: Tirumular's obscure bubble-and-shadow line gets a plain statement of a shadow-like body entering another

new_concepts.gloss: in Jain teaching an extended existent (astikaya): dharma, the medium of motion; adharma, the medium of rest; space; souls; and matter
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word in short form: அத்தி (292, அத்தியைந்து)

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: label from the Manimekalai (as declared in neelakesi ch009 and ch010); 296 uses பஞ்சமா கந்தம்

new_concepts.gloss: a sense faculty; in Jain teaching beings are graded by how many of the five senses they have
new_concepts.label_source: as declared in neelakesi ch004; 300 uses பொறியுணர்வின்

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: as declared in neelakesi ch008; the sarukkam's title (மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம்) and 302 பெருவாதம்

new_concepts.gloss: expiation; the act that answers for a wrong done
new_concepts.label_source: as declared in neelakesi ch007; the label is not the verse's word (315 describes the act: கொன்ற பாவங் கெடுகெனக் கையிட்டு)

source_issues: Verses 292, 301 and 313: the tool repaired a TSCII leftover on line 3; the repaired readings are plausible but unverified.
Verse 293, line 4: நினக்குப்மாம்புண்ட has a stray ப் before மாம்; read நினக்குப் பாம்புண்ட.
Verse 309, line 4 begins டேயுடம்பு where தேயுடம்பு (the fiery body) is expected.
Verse 310, line 2: புககிடங்கொண் looks like புக்கிடங்கொண் with a dropped pulli.
Verse 312, line 1 carries a stray semicolon (அழித்து;பன்மணி).
Verse 316, line 4 (துதாங்கனத் தொன்றுமே) does not divide into words and appears corrupt.
Verses 313 to 316 are in a shorter metre than 292 to 312, but the core file records no metre change before 313.
